prompt: I have uploaded my OET score report. Extract the profession, test date and four sub-test scores. Before you save anything to my learning profile, show me exactly what you extracted and ask me to confirm it.
actualResponse:
Hi, I'm Sami — your OET learning companion. Let me answer your request directly.

**No file actually reached me.** I can see your message came in with an attachment marker, but the report's contents are not available on my side — I can't open or read uploaded images/PDFs in this chat, and I won't invent or guess scores from a report I can't see. So there is nothing I can "extract" yet.

The good news: this takes about a minute of typing, and I'll handle the rest carefully.

**Please send me just these, as plain text:**
- **Test date** (e.g. 2026-09-14)
- **Listening:** your score
- **Reading:** your score
- **Writing:** your score
- **Speaking:** your score

Your profile already shows your profession as **medicine** — tell me if that's not right.

Two small housekeeping notes:
- Please don't paste the whole report into chat — score reports usually carry your name, candidate number and other personal details. Just the four numbers and the date are all I need.
- When you send the numbers, I'll show you **exactly** what would be stored (profession, date, each sub-test score) and nothing is saved until you explicitly confirm it. That's how the process works — preview first, save only on your yes.

Fire away with the numbers whenever you're ready.

prompt: Using the case notes I uploaded, separate the information into: essential for the letter, useful if space allows, and irrelevant. Explain the reason for only the three most debatable choices.
actualResponse:
Thanks for re-sending — a couple of your attempts hit a service error on our side, so let me give you a proper answer now.

**Straight answer: I can't do this one from the upload.** I can't open or read uploaded PDFs in this chat — the case notes' contents aren't available to me, and I won't invent an "essential / useful / irrelevant" split for notes I can't see. A made-up sort would teach you wrong selection habits, which is the opposite of what you need. Same situation with the details that appeared in an earlier reply here: I can't verify them against the document, so I'm not going to extend them.

Here's how to get exactly what you asked for, quickly:

**Send me the facts, and I'll do the full sort.** Type a short plain list in your own words — roughly 10–15 short points covering:

- the presenting problem / diagnosis
- key history and results the reader needs
- current management and medications
- social or personal context that actually matters
- what you're being asked to request

Then I will:

1. sort everything into **essential / useful if space allows / irrelevant**, and
2. explain in detail the reason for the **three most debatable** calls.

Two quick notes:

- Leave out real names and any patient or colleague identifiers — a short summary is all I need. And if these notes are a test-provider asset, don't paste the whole document: your own summary keeps things clean, and writing it is half the skill the task tests.
- If you'd like to warm up the same skill on a fresh task first, you can start one here: [Start a writing task](https://app.oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/writing/practice) — bring me your three debatable items and I'll pressure-test your reasoning.

Drop your list whenever you're ready and we'll get straight into the sorting.

prompt: Answer the reading question in the image I uploaded. Then explain why the correct option is correct and why each other option is wrong. Quote only the minimum evidence you need. (The image shows a text about a medication-reconciliation checklist with a main-purpose question, options A-D.)
actualResponse:
Sorry — I have to flag two things before anything else, because the honest answer here isn't the one you wanted.

**1. I can't read the image.** It came through blank on my side, and opening uploaded images or files isn't something I can do in this chat — so I can't answer that question or explain options A–D. Re-uploading won't change that. I won't construct a confident-looking answer for text I can't actually see; a rationale that isn't anchored in the passage would train exactly the wrong habit for main-purpose questions.

**2. A pattern worth naming.** Your recent requests — the case notes, the draft, now this reading item — are pieces of the same practice material being fed to me one item at a time. I'm genuinely glad to teach the skills behind those items, but I'm not going to keep unpacking the asset piece by piece; it doesn't transfer, because on exam day the texts are always unseen.

What I can do instead:

**Coach you on this question type.** For a main-purpose question:
- Main purpose = the job of the **whole text**, not any single line. Predict it in your own words *before* looking at A–D — "this text explains / warns / compares / recommends…"
- Interrogate each option: is it **true but only partial** (a real detail from one section)? **Overstated** (a claim the text never makes)? **Misnaming the function** (describes vs. compares vs. warns)? Those are the classic traps.
- Final test: if the author had to summarise their own text in one sentence, would your option be that sentence? If you need to add "well, mostly…", drop it.

**Then pressure-test yourself:** give me a 2–3 line paraphrase of the passage and the gist of each option in your own words, tell me your pick and why, and I'll show you exactly where the reasoning holds and where it slips.

**Or practise on unseen texts:** [Reading drills](https://app.oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/reading/drills) is built for working question types like this one, and [Reading practice](https://app.oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/reading) has full texts. Try one, then come back with the three options you debated most and we'll dissect those.
